rv.q: Mr. Lithgow, under the unerringly precise direction of the veteran Nicholas Hytner, does not shy away from any of his repellent aspects, bringing each to bruising and, thankfully, often scabrously funny life in a performance that’s a mesmerizing highlight of the theater season.
Giant, thrilling and abrasive, is full of rewards.

Lithgow — so nimble and charismatic and then suddenly so imposing, with no aversion to the grotesque — knows how to bring out the insecurity that almost always festers at the center of any performatively self-certain action.
It’s a provocative study in the ongoing challenge of asking giants to watch their step.
Navigating his moods is, for the other characters on stage (including his pained fiancée Liccy, played by Rachael Stirling) a challenge; for the audience, it is a thought-provoking pleasure.
In this case, of course, recent events in Iran only have made the play seem more timely.

In Rosenblatt’s play, he is a BFG (Big Fractious Giant): The real man was 6-foot-6, while Lithgow is 6-foot-3. The director Nicholas Hytner keeps Dahl’s height in reserve, almost as if it’s a special effect. When the curtain rises, Lithgow is seated.
It’s Lithgow’s ability to be quiet and sweet and seconds later booming and scary that makes us squirm in our seats over our own feelings toward the writer.
You won’t see a more powerful play this season, or a more important one.
A bold, provocative, and thoroughly gripping piece of theatre.
The masterfully written and thrillingly performed drama depicts Dahl obstinately refusing to extinguish a fire of his own making.
The quibbles hardly matter considering Lithgow's towering performance, which blends warmth and ugliness in fascinating fashion.
Maybe it’s asking too much of an already terrific play to tackle these questions, too.
If the play is about the failed genius, Rosenblatt spends entirely too much time on antisemitism, and if it is about antisemitism, there is far too much meaningless banter.
Rosenblatt’s script approaches these issues with intelligence and restraint.
While admirably smart and ably directed by Nicholas Hytner, Giant shrinks from the nagging fact that it goes in circles rather than building in gripping dramatic fashion.
But Rosenblatt is a brave and intelligent playwright willing to take on a subject that no one else seems willing to touch.

For all its dramatic pleasures and gestures towards nuance, Giant winds up feeling like the latest example of a type of weaponized censorship that deems any criticism of governments as human-scale hate speech.
Lithgow delivers a real feast for theatergoers.
It's a powerful wallop of a work with a performance by John Lithgow that packs an equally reverberating wallop.
He’s horrifying, fascinating, and devastating all at once.
The two-time Tony winner not only rises to the occasion, he towers over it, both literally and figuratively.
Regardless of these minor shortcomings “Giant” is a Broadway show not to be missed this season, due primarily to the “Giant” performance by the magnificent John Lithgow.
That, on its own, is worth a trip.
What makes the work sing is its refusal to resort to caricature, humanizing Dahl through his fiancée

tn.cat: Best Featured Actress in a Play

cn.t: Lithgow delivers a towering, fearless performance as Roald Dahl in this timely drama about the beloved author's antisemitism, but critics find the play itself preachy and overly earnest despite its sharp relevance and strong cast.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.

vr.q: Watching how a character reveals himself as the stakes of a situation become higher and more personal is incredibly captivating, and John Lithgow's performance is rightfully the centerpiece of the whole show.
I think it's worth seeing for his performance and just for the history... but to me the play felt more like the writer didn't find a clever way to really explore this subject.
